# The editions {.unnumbered}

Philidor's book was rewritten twice by its author and translated many times
over, and the copies that survive do not all say the same thing. Two lines
descend from 1749: one in French, one in English. This transcription follows
the English line. A reader comparing a copy from the French line should expect
differences, and some are substantial.

{{< include _includes/editions-timeline.md >}}

## What each edition is

Where a statement here rests on the scans themselves it is marked **[scan]**;
everything else is sourced below. The distinction matters: a title page is
evidence, a bookseller's description is a claim.

**1749 — *L'Analyze des Échecs*, London, in French.** Philidor was living in
England and published in his own language. Three printings carry the date
1749.^[[ChessBase, *Philidor's* L'Analyze des Echecs](https://en.chessbase.com/post/philidor-s-l-analyze-des-echecs)] Its rule on promotion was stricter than what followed: a
pawn could be exchanged only for a piece already captured — which the 1777
records in a marginal note about its own earlier edition **[scan]**.

**1777 — two books in one year.** *Analyse du jeu des échecs, nouvelle édition,
considérablement augmentée* in French,^[[*Analyse du jeu des échecs*, Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_analyse-du-jeu-des-chec_philidor-f-d-franco_1777)] and *Analysis of the
Game of Chess* in English. The English one is the **base text of this
transcription**. Its title page reads "A NEW EDITION, GREATLY ENLARGED. By A. D.
PHILIDOR ... LONDON: Printed for P. ELMSLEY, in the STRAND. MDCCLXXVII"
**[scan]**. It reprints the 1749 material with corrections and adds the
supplement, the Gambit of Salvio, the ends of parties, and seventeen rules of
the game **[scan]**. Booksellers describe it as possibly the first chess book
published in English;^[a description repeated in dealers' listings of the 1777; their claim, not one checked here] that is their claim, not one this project
can check.

**1790 — *Analysis of the Game of Chess*, "a new edition, improved and greatly
enlarged", in two volumes.** Used here for **collation**. Its title page adds
"TO WHICH IS ADDED, SEVERAL PARTIES, PLAYED BY THE AUTHOR BLINDFOLD, AGAINST
THREE ADVERSARIES", and the imprint is again P. Elmsly in the Strand, M·DCC·XC
**[scan]**. Only volume I is to hand: the copy ends "END OF THE FIRST VOLUME"
**[scan]**, and it holds the parties and gambits. Volume II held the ends of
parties, which is why chapters 70 to 98 here have never been read against a
second source.

**1819 — Philidor by way of W. S. Kenny, London, printed for T. and J.
Allman.** *Illustrated by diagrams, on which are marked the situation of the
party for the back-games and ends of parties; with critical remarks and notes
by the author of the "Stratagems of Chess". Translated from the last French
edition, and further illustrated with notes, by W. S. Kenny.*^[Powell's;
HathiTrust] Sold by Baldwin, Cradock and Joy, Paternoster Row, and Bell and
Bradfute, Edinburgh. Catalogued as the first edition of this
translation.^[[Christie's, lot 3508267](https://www.christies.com.cn/en/lot/lot-3508267)] William Stopford Kenny (1788–1867) had already
published *Practical Chess Grammar* (1817) and *Practical Chess Exercises*
(1818).^[[Bernard Quaritch Ltd, stock GU29](https://www.quaritch.com/books/philidor-fran%C3%A7ois-andr%C3%A9-danican-william-stopford-k/analysis-of-the-game-of-chess-illustrated-by-diagr/GU29/)] It carries seventeen rules, as the 1777 does — reported by
the owner of the copy, not seen here.

The book went on being reprinted long after: something like seventy editions by
1871, and translations into German and Italian.^[[ChessBase, *Philidor's* L'Analyze des Echecs](https://en.chessbase.com/post/philidor-s-l-analyze-des-echecs)]

## Why a French-line copy differs

The 1819 is not a reprint of the English 1777 or 1790. It comes down the other
branch, from a French edition Philidor had gone on revising, and it arrives
through a translator who added material of his own. Between the English 1777
and Kenny's French source lie forty years of the author's second thoughts and
somebody else's editing.

That is enough to account for what a comparison turns up, and the differences
found so far are of three kinds, none of them a fault in either book:

- **The same study, a different verdict.** From `3k4/3p4/4r3/3K4/8/1Q6/8/8`,
  the 1777 gives four moves and calls the game drawn; the 1819 heads it "A
  check mate with a queen against a Castle and a Pawn" and gives eighteen moves
  ending in mate.
- **The same study, a different board.** At the 4th move of the first
  back-game of the rook and bishop against a rook, the 1819 has the black king
  on d8 where this text has him on e8.
- **A different arrangement.** What is one study in one edition may be a study
  and a back-game in the other, so the numbering does not line up.

A fourth kind is worth naming separately, because it runs the other way: the
1819 **confirmed** a reading here. It puts a white queen on b3 in the drawn
game against a rook and a pawn, which is where the text says she stands and
where this transcription had failed to put her.

Both editions also use "castle" and "rook" for the same piece, which is only a
matter of the translator's English.

Open questions from the comparison are kept in the repository's `TODO.md`.

## A word on the rules

The 1777 closes with the seventeen rules of the Chess Club in England, and they
are not the modern ones. Under that code a stalemated player **won** the game
in England, though not in France; promotion had been restricted to a captured
piece in the 1749 edition; and the fifty-move rule was something you claimed
rather than something that happened. Where Philidor calls a position won or
drawn, that is the code he is judging it under. The repository's `RULES.md`
sets them out.

The 1819 carries seventeen rules as well, so the code travelled down the French
line and through the translation intact in number at least. Whether it survived
unchanged in substance is worth knowing, and rule XVI is the one to look at,
because an 1819 book sits exactly on the change.

The English rule stood from about 1600 to 1800. The London Chess Club rejected
Philidor's version at its founding in 1807, and Sarratt's *Treatise* of 1808
gives the modern one in its rule 24: "If the King be stale-mate, the game is a
drawn game." The draw was widely accepted in England by the early
1820s.^[Edward Winter, [*Stalemate*](https://www.chesshistory.com/winter/extra/stalemate.html), citing the London Chess Club of 1807 and Sarratt's *Treatise* of 1808] Kenny's book falls between the two, so which rule it prints is
not predictable — and it decides whether the endgame verdicts in the two
editions were reached under the same law at all.


## Sources

Marked **[scan]** above: read directly from the two scans this project works
from, which are described in the repository's README.

- **ChessBase** — ["Philidor's *L'Analyze des Echecs*"](https://en.chessbase.com/post/philidor-s-l-analyze-des-echecs),
  for the three printings of 1749 and the later reprinting history.
- **Internet Archive** — [*Analyse du jeu des échecs*, 1777, in French](https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_analyse-du-jeu-des-chec_philidor-f-d-franco_1777),
  and [*L'analyze des echecs*, 1749](https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_lanalyze-des-echecs-co_philidor-f-d-franco_1749_0).
- **Christie's** — [lot description for the 1819 Kenny](https://www.christies.com.cn/en/lot/lot-3508267),
  giving it as the first edition of that translation.
- **Quaritch** — [catalogue entry for the 1819](https://www.quaritch.com/books/philidor-fran%C3%A7ois-andr%C3%A9-danican-william-stopford-k/analysis-of-the-game-of-chess-illustrated-by-diagr/GU29/),
  for Kenny's dates and his earlier books.
- **Powell's / HathiTrust** — [the full 1819 title](https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/008591460),
  including the notes by the author of the *Stratagems of Chess*.
- **Winter** — Edward Winter, ["Stalemate"](https://www.chesshistory.com/winter/extra/stalemate.html),
  for the English rule, its rejection by the London Chess Club in 1807, and
  Sarratt's *Treatise* of 1808.
- **bookseller** — the "first chess book in English" description appears in
  dealers' listings of the 1777; it is repeated here as their claim.

The comparisons with the 1819 come from its owner, who is reading a physical
copy; they are recorded as reported, and the open ones are in the repository's
`TODO.md`.
